Speculative decoding is a technique designed to accelerate text generation by leveraging the fact that large language models are often deterministic in their predictions. The core idea is to introduce a smaller, faster "draft" model to propose a sequence of tokens, which a larger, more accurate "target" model then verifies.

The process begins with the draft model generating a short sequence of tokens, such as five words, in parallel. This is significantly faster than the target model generating those same tokens one by one. The target model then evaluates this entire proposed sequence at once. If the target model agrees with the draft model’s prediction for all tokens in the sequence, the entire block is accepted, and the process repeats. This effectively allows the system to generate multiple tokens in a single forward pass of the slower model, rather than waiting for each token to be generated sequentially.

If the target model disagrees with the draft model at any point in the sequence, it identifies the first mismatch. The system then accepts all tokens up to that point and regenerates the remaining sequence starting from the mismatched token. This ensures that the final output is identical to what the target model would have produced if it had generated the text token by token from the beginning. The draft model’s role is purely to guess ahead; the target model acts as the ground truth, ensuring accuracy.

This method does not change the underlying logic or the final text produced by the primary model. It simply optimizes the computational path. By batching the verification of multiple tokens, speculative decoding reduces the number of times the slower, more resource-intensive target model needs to perform a full forward pass. The speedup comes from parallelizing the draft generation and minimizing the number of sequential steps required for the target model. As long as the draft model is sufficiently aligned with the target model, the overhead of verification is low, and the overall generation time is reduced without sacrificing the quality or content of the output.

plain.content:
You are already familiar with autoregressive text generation: the large model looks at everything it has produced so far, samples the next token, appends it, and repeats. That sequential loop is where the latency lives, because you cannot run step *n*+1 until step *n* is done. Speculative decoding attacks exactly that bottleneck without touching the model, the prompt, or the sampling distribution.

Here is the mechanism. Before the large model ever runs, a second, much smaller model is already sitting on the same GPU. The small model takes the current prefix and greedily proposes, say, eight tokens in a single forward pass. Because it is small, that pass finishes in a fraction of the time the large model would need to generate even one token autoregressively.

Next, the large model runs once over the *entire* sequence of proposed tokens. Crucially, it computes its probability distribution for every token in that window simultaneously. It is not doing eight sequential steps; it is doing one forward pass that gives you eight outputs at once. At each position the large model compares its own predicted token against the small model's proposal. As long as the match holds, you keep the proposed tokens and have just jumped eight positions ahead. The moment you hit a mismatch, you discard everything from that position onward and resume autoregressive generation from the last agreed token.

This is why the output is identical to what the large model would have produced on its own. The large model has never been asked to sample from a different distribution; it has always seen the same prefix and always sampled from its own logits. Speculative decoding has only reordered the work: the small model supplies a cheap hypothesis, and the large model merely validates it in batch. When the small model is right, you saved an entire forward pass of the large model for free. When it is wrong, the cost of that one forward pass is comparable to a normal autoregressive step, so you lose almost nothing.

In practice the small model agrees with the large one for most proposed tokens, so you can reduce the number of large-model forward passes from one per output token to roughly one per six or seven output tokens. The text you print is, for all intents and purposes, the exact text the large model would have written one token at a time.

plain.content:
When you insert a key-value pair into a hash map, the hash function first takes your key and crunches it down into a single integer index. That index points to a specific slot in the map's underlying array. Collisions happen whenever two different keys produce the same index — which is statistically inevitable once you're storing a meaningful number of items, even with a well-designed hash function.

The most common way a hash map deals with this is called separate chaining. At each slot in the internal array, instead of holding a single key-value pair, it holds a small linked list (or chain) of pairs. When you try to insert a new item and its computed index already contains an entry, the new item is simply appended to that existing list rather than replacing anything. Lookups work the same way: the hash points you to the right slot, and you then scan through that short chain linearly to confirm whether the exact key is present. Because a good hash function spreads items out, each chain stays very short in practice — often just one or two elements long — so the linear search step is negligible in cost.

A second, less frequently used strategy is open addressing, where the array slot itself is the only storage, and on a collision the map probes for the next available slot using a deterministic formula. Linear probing steps one slot at a time; quadratic probing skips in increasing intervals; double hashing uses a second independent hash to determine the step size. This approach avoids the overhead of maintaining per-slot linked lists but has its own quirks in how deletions must be handled and how performance degrades as the array fills up, which is why chaining is the more widespread default in most standard library implementations.

Resizing, or rehashing, is the mechanism by which the map keeps its performance within an acceptable range. The map tracks a load factor, which is simply the ratio of stored items to the total number of available slots. Once that ratio crosses a predefined threshold — commonly around 0.75 in many standard implementations, though some choose different values — the map knows the average chain length (or clustering in the open-addressing case) is starting to grow and that the cost of each operation is creeping upward toward linear rather than staying near-constant.

At that point, on the next insert, the map allocates a new internal array that is typically double the size of the old one. It then takes every key-value pair from the old structure, recomputes its hash index, and places it into the corresponding slot of the new array, rebuilding all the chains fresh. The old array is then discarded and its memory is freed. Because every item is rehashed and the number of slots has doubled, the average chain length drops back down to near its original low level, and the load factor returns to a healthy, small number. This resize operation is amortized across all the inserts that built up to it, so any individual insert is, on average, constant-time even though this particular one took longer. The process repeats over the life of the map as it continues to grow, each time the current array fills past its threshold again.

If you've run a large language model on the standard autoregressive path, you know it's bottlenecked by the fact that it generates one token at a time. Every single token requires a full forward pass through the network, and those passes must be done sequentially because each new token depends on all the previous ones. For a model with billions of parameters on a single GPU, each of those passes takes a noticeable amount of time, and multiplying that out over thousands of tokens makes the whole process feel glacial.

Speculative decoding is a trick that breaks this wall without changing the output at all. The core idea is to run two models in concert. First, a small, fast model that you already have on hand predicts a short sequence of tokens — say, ten or twenty — all in a fast forward pass. This is your "draft." Next, you hand that entire sequence to the large model and ask it to evaluate all of those tokens in a single forward pass, using the draft as context. Because the large model processes all of those positions in parallel, that verification step only costs roughly one forward pass no matter how long the draft sequence is.

Here is why the output is unchanged. The large model is the one that decides what to keep. It computes the same probability distribution over each candidate token it would have if it were running autoregressively from scratch. As long as the large model assigns a sufficiently high probability to each drafted token in sequence, you accept all of them at once and have effectively jumped ahead by several tokens at the cost of only one additional large-model pass. If the large model disagrees with any token, you simply accept everything up to that point and resume. The small model's role is purely to suggest candidates; it never determines the final answer.

The speedup comes from the fact that you've replaced several sequential large-model passes with one parallel verification pass, and you do this over and over. In practice, with a well-matched small draft model, this can cut total generation time by a factor of two to three without a single character in the output being different from what a pure autoregressive run would produce.

plain.content:
When two different keys happen to produce the same hash value, that hash map has to decide where to store both. The most common approach is called separate chaining. Each slot in the underlying array holds not a single value but a small linked list (or similar structure). When a key lands in an already-occupied slot, the new entry is simply appended to that list. During a lookup, the map computes the hash, jumps to that slot, and then walks down the short list comparing keys until it finds a match or reaches the end. The list stays short under normal conditions because the hash function should distribute keys evenly, so most slots end up holding zero or one item. A second family of approaches is known as open addressing, in which the table has no per-slot lists. Instead, when the initially computed slot is taken, the map probes for the next available position using a fixed formula, such as moving one slot further each time, jumping by quadratic steps, or using a second hash function to determine the step size. With open addressing you must ensure the probe sequence is long enough to always eventually find a free slot, which means the table is never allowed to become completely full.

Either way, if the map keeps accumulating entries without any growth, things degrade. With chaining the lists get longer, turning what should be a constant-time lookup into a slow linear scan. With open addressing the probing steps grow longer because the table fills up and you bounce between occupied slots more and more times before landing on an empty one. So the map tracks a ratio of used slots to total available slots, called the load factor. Once that ratio crosses a predefined threshold, typically somewhere around 0.7 or 0.75, the map triggers a resize.

During a resize, the map allocates a new internal array, almost always double the old capacity, so that the ratio drops back down to a manageable level. Every existing key-value pair is then re-inserted into this new, larger structure. Each key gets its hash recomputed modulo the new size, which means every entry lands at a potentially different index than before. This is the one operation in a hash map that is genuinely expensive, O(n) in the number of entries, because it touches every item in the table. Resizing is therefore not something the map does on every single insert; it's a relatively rare event that gets paid for over time. If the map ever starts with too many deletions, some implementations also check the reverse ratio and will shrink the table back down when a very large fraction of slots are empty, to avoid holding onto a wastefully oversized array indefinitely. The practical upshot is that you get amortized constant-time operations for individual inserts, lookups, and deletions, with the occasional costly full rehash spread across many operations so that the average cost per operation stays effectively the same.
